name: Sabudana Khichdi
cuisine: Maharashtrian (upvas / vrat dish, also an everyday Mumbai breakfast)

ingredients.name: Water, for soaking
ingredients.householdMeasure: about ⅓ cup (just enough to sit level with the pearls)

ingredients.name: Peanuts (moongphali / shengdana), raw or already roasted
Potato (aloo / batata)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ medium potato, in 1 cm cubes

equipment: Mixing bowl (for washing and soaking) and a lid or plate to cover it
Heavy-bottomed or non-stick kadai or frying pan (8 inch) with a lid
Small pan or tawa to dry-roast the peanuts (or buy ready roasted peanuts)
Mortar and pestle (khalbatta) to crush the peanuts
Spatula (flat, wooden or silicone), knife and chopping board
Measuring cup and spoons (a normal teacup and teaspoons are fine stand-ins)

steps.title: Measure the sabudana
steps.text: Put 75 g (about ½ cup) sabudana in a bowl.
steps.tip: Buy "medium" or "nylon" sabudana for khichdi. Very small pearls turn mushy; very large ones need a longer soak.
steps.visualCue: A small heap of dry, white pearls.
steps.cameraCheck: The ½ cup of sabudana in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Dry pearls pouring into a steel bowl.

steps.title: Wash out the starch
steps.text: Cover the pearls with water, rub them gently between your fingers for a few seconds, and pour off the cloudy water. Repeat 3–4 times.
steps.tip: This is the first half of the "non-sticky pearls" trick. The milky water is loose starch; if it stays, it glues the pearls together when cooked.
steps.visualCue: The water is clear or only very slightly cloudy on the last rinse.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl with the clear rinse water
steps.videoShot: Fingers rubbing pearls in milky water, then the water being poured away.

steps.title: Soak with just a little water
steps.text: Drain completely, then add 80–90 ml water (about ⅓ cup), just enough to sit level with the top of the pearls, not above them. Cover and leave on the counter.
steps.tip: This is the second half of the trick: less water, longer time. Too much water makes soggy, sticky pearls. Different brands absorb differently, so note what works for yours.
steps.visualCue: All the water is absorbed and the pearls have swollen to about double their size.
steps.cameraCheck: The water level with the pearls before covering
steps.videoShot: Water poured in just up to the pearl line, then the lid going on.

steps.title: Check the soak
steps.text: Press one pearl between your thumb and finger.
steps.tip: Still a hard centre? Sprinkle 1–2 tbsp water, cover and wait 30 min more. Water pooling at the bottom? Tip it into a strainer and let it drain for 10 min.
steps.visualCue: It squashes easily with no hard white dot in the centre. The pearls look separate and slightly glossy, not sitting in water.
steps.cameraCheck: A squashed pearl on your fingertip
steps.videoShot: A pearl being pressed flat between two fingers.

steps.title: Fluff the pearls
steps.text: Run a fork or your fingers through the soaked sabudana to separate any clumps.
steps.visualCue: Loose, individual pearls that fall apart when you lift a handful.
steps.videoShot: Fingers lifting and dropping fluffy pearls.

steps.title: Roast the peanuts
steps.text: Dry-roast 25 g raw peanuts in a small pan on medium-low heat, stirring often. (Skip this if they are already roasted.)
steps.visualCue: The skins crack and darken in spots, and they smell nutty.
steps.cameraCheck: The roasted peanuts in the pan
steps.videoShot: Peanuts tossing in a dry pan, skins starting to blister.

steps.title: Cool and crush the peanuts
steps.text: Let them cool for a minute, rub off the loose skins if you like, then crush them coarsely in a mortar and pestle.
steps.visualCue: A coarse powder with some small chunks, still dry and crumbly (not oily paste).
steps.cameraCheck: The crushed peanuts in the mortar
steps.videoShot: The pestle pounding peanuts into coarse crumbs.

steps.title: Mix peanuts, salt and sugar into the sabudana
steps.text: Add the crushed peanuts, ¼ tsp sendha namak and ½ tsp sugar to the soaked pearls and toss lightly with your fingers.
steps.tip: Coating the pearls before they hit the pan (a step most Maharashtrian recipes use) keeps them separate and seasons them evenly.
steps.visualCue: Every pearl is lightly coated with peanut powder.
steps.cameraCheck: The coated sabudana in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Peanut crumbs sprinkled over the pearls and tossed through.

steps.title: Cut the potato
steps.text: Peel ½ medium potato (60 g) and cut it into small 1 cm cubes. Rinse and pat dry.
steps.cameraCheck: The potato cubes on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife dicing a potato half.

steps.title: Chop the chilli and coriander
steps.text: Finely chop 1 green chilli and 1 tbsp coriander leaves. Keep 5–6 curry leaves ready.
steps.visualCue: Small chilli rings or bits, a little heap of coriander.
steps.cameraCheck: The chopped chilli, coriander and curry leaves
steps.videoShot: Overhead shot of the small heaps on the board.

steps.title: Heat the ghee and crackle the cumin
steps.text: Heat the kadai on medium, add 2 tsp ghee, then ½ tsp cumin seeds.
steps.visualCue: The cumin sizzles and turns one shade darker within about 20 seconds.
steps.videoShot: Cumin seeds sizzling in melted ghee.

steps.title: Add the chilli and curry leaves
steps.text: Add the green chilli and curry leaves and stir.
steps.tip: Stand back a little; wet curry leaves splatter.
steps.visualCue: The curry leaves crackle and turn glossy; a sharp chilli smell rises.
steps.cameraCheck: The kadai with chilli and leaves
steps.videoShot: Curry leaves spluttering in the pan.

steps.title: Cook the potato
steps.text: Add the potato cubes, stir, cover and cook on low-medium heat, stirring once or twice.
steps.tip: Cutting the potato small means it cooks raw in the pan. If you have a boiled potato, cube it and fry it for just 1 min instead.
steps.visualCue: The potato is soft when pressed with the spatula and lightly golden on some sides.
steps.cameraCheck: A potato cube pressed with the spatula
steps.videoShot: The lid lifting off golden potato cubes.

steps.title: Add the sabudana
steps.text: Turn the heat to low, add the peanut-coated sabudana and fold it in gently with the spatula, lifting from the bottom.
steps.visualCue: Pearls, potato and spices are evenly mixed; the pearls are still white.
steps.videoShot: The spatula folding the pearls into the potatoes.

steps.title: Cook until the pearls turn see-through
steps.text: Keep on low heat, stirring gently every 30 seconds. Cover for 1 minute in between if your pan is not non-stick.
steps.tip: Stop as soon as most pearls turn clear. Overcooking is the other main reason sabudana khichdi goes chewy and lumpy; the leftover white centres finish cooking from the heat once the gas is off.
steps.visualCue: Most pearls turn translucent (glassy) with only a faint white centre; they look glossy and stay separate.
steps.videoShot: Close-up of white pearls turning glassy.

steps.title: Finish with lemon and coriander
steps.text: Switch off the heat. Add 1 tsp lemon juice and the chopped coriander and toss gently.
steps.visualCue: Green flecks through glossy, separate pearls; it smells of ghee and peanuts.
steps.cameraCheck: The finished khichdi in the pan

steps.title: Taste and serve
steps.text: Taste and add a pinch of sendha namak or sugar if needed. Serve hot on a plate.
steps.visualCue: Fluffy, glistening pearls with peanut crumbs and golden potato bits.
steps.videoShot: Khichdi spooned onto a plate next to a bowl of curd.

reasons: no deep-frying, a modest 2 tsp ghee, and peanuts add some protein, fibre and good fats. But sabudana is close to pure refined starch with a high glycaemic index and almost no protein or micronutrients, so the plate is filling for a short time and then leaves you hungry; it is about 560 kcal with only about 8 g protein. Restaurant versions are often greasy (reviewers have called some Mumbai versions oily) with 1 tbsp+ of ghee or oil per plate.

researchRating.basis: one of the best-known Maharashtrian dishes and the default fasting food across western and northern India, featured in nearly every "best Maharashtrian breakfast in Mumbai" guide (LBB, Homegrown, Curly Tales) and served at classic Mumbai spots such as Prakash (Dadar), Aaswad (Dadar), Panshikar (Girgaum) and Ladu Samrat (Lalbaug). Recipes are well reviewed (Hebbar's Kitchen 5/5 from 194 votes; Whisk Affair 4.75/5; Ministry of Curry 4.67/5), and many recipe pages are built around fixing sticky results. Small deduction because it is easy to get wrong (sticky or chewy) and many people find it heavy.

storage: Best eaten fresh; the pearls harden and turn chewy as they cool. Fridge: up to 1 day in an airtight box, within 2 hours of cooking. Freezing is not recommended (the pearls go rubbery and the potato grainy). To reheat, sprinkle 1–2 tsp water, cover and microwave for 1 min, or warm in a covered non-stick pan on low heat for 2–3 min, stirring gently.
leftoverRemix: Sabudana vada / tikki. Mash 1 cup leftover khichdi with 1 small boiled potato and a few extra crushed peanuts, shape into 4 flat patties, and shallow-fry them on a tawa with 1 tsp ghee or oil per side until crisp and golden (or air-fry at 190 °C for about 12 min). Serve with green chutney or curd: a crispy snack from soft leftovers.
burnOff: about 8.0 km of running (560 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 11 km of brisk walking (about 2 h 15 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). A bowl of curd on the side adds about 1–1.5 km of running.

navratri.reason: sabudana, peanuts, potato, green chilli, cumin and sendha namak (rock salt, already used in this recipe) are standard upvas foods; assumes the common Maharashtrian/North Indian rule set, and some families also skip cumin or curry leaves.

ekadashi.reason: a classic Ekadashi dish with no rice, wheat, pulses, onion, garlic or table salt; peanuts and potato are generally allowed, though some strict sampradayas have extra rules.

jain.reason: skip the potato (root vegetable) and add more peanuts; Swiggy Mumbai lists a "Jain" sabudana khichdi, but practice on sabudana itself (a cassava-starch product) varies by family.

ramadan.reason: vegetarian, so there is no halal concern; it is mostly quick-digesting starch, so for sehri serve it with curd and the peanuts for staying power; also a common light iftar plate.
